Workers in the mines will experience noise levels above 70 dB when laboring near operating equipment. When the level exceeds 90 dB, exposure of more than 8 hours can result in occupational hearing damage. If sound levels are 95 decibels, hearing damage risk occurs with 4 or more hours exposure. The noise effects can be mitigated if the workers wear plugs or ear covers. Unfortunately, there may be a tendency toward carelessness, and some workers may not always use hearing protection devices.
People living near the spur lines will be annoyed by noise from the unit train.
Social Impacts
The additional income from coal development may create change in life styles, social habits and concepts which will be disruptive to existing Crow and non-Crow social patterns and structures. The introduction of new ways of life and the trend toward urbanization will require social and cultural adjustments by members of the Tribe as well as non-Crow members of the impact area.
Under any set of development (or lack of development) circumstances the resident population of the Crow Tribe is expected to more than double between 1970 and 2000. Depending on the development circumstance and the Crow labor force participation rate the differences in impacts between the low and high level production rates are expected to be minimal. However, with other coal development in the region the permanent non-Crow population could increase by amounts ranging from 2263 to 2547 while total populations increases for the entire impact area would range from 7869 to 8152 resulting in a near doubling of total population. Such population increases can have adverse impacts upon life styles, social habits, and culture of the residents even with proper planning and regulated development.
